description.narrative: Funding to Geoscience Australia to support Digital Earth Africa which provides African countries with access to free and open information available from satellite images relating to flooding, drought, soil and coastal erosion, agriculture, forest cover, land use and land cover change, water availability and quality, and changes to human settlements. Digital Earth Africa Phase III will create additional value from the science, technology, and institutional arrangements established in Phase II, by driving uptake of the program and delivering impact in Africa.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: DEA presented a set of capacity-building workshops in Madagascar to show the importance of earth observation in the management of critical environmental resources. With its unique ecosystems and rich biodiversity, the island must ensure sustainable environmental management. The country holds nine percent of Africa’s mangrove forests, which capture carbon, host biodiversity and are flood defences. Mining accounts for 32% of the total exports. ‍ Participants were introduced to the Digital Earth Africa Sandbox, which comes with well-described steps (known as notebooks) and analysis-ready datasets that are accessible to those without coding experience. Participants studied Madagascar’s water resources; natural vegetation; the expansion and geographical impact of mining activities and natural vegetation, and crop health monitoring. ‍ By comparing imagery with the Global Mangrove Watch Database, participants ascertained that mangrove vegetation in Madagascar appears to be stable except for pockets around human settlements.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: Digital Earth Africa (DE Africa) participated in Africa Climate Week September 2023 in Nairobi. The event provided a platform for policymakers, practitioners, businesses, and civil society to discuss climate solutions and informed the first global stocktake concluding at COP28 in UAE in December 2023. ‍ The Information for Agriculture, Food and Water Security project promoted at Climate Week sought to improve the productivity of smallholder farmers. The one-year exploratory project was funded by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research and led by DEA. Time-series Earth observation data allowed generation of statistics to leverage effective planning and monitoring, leading to better food and water security outcomes. The outcome of the project was to design a Roadmap for Digital Earth Africa for fit-for-purpose co-development of solutions focused on agriculture, food and water security for across the continent.

description.narrative: In 2024, Digital Earth Africa (DE Africa) supported 22 African countries through training, institutional partnerships, and operational use cases. ‍ DE Africa conducted 22 training sessions across 8 countries: Congo, Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi, South Africa, Tunisia, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. 945 individuals from across 22 different institutions (6 government agencies, 7 non-governmental organisations, and 8 academic institutions) participated. 502 training completion certificates have been awarded, and DEA platform users grew to >29,000 DE Africa Maps users and >6,500 Sandbox users. ‍ DE Africa Implementing Partners provided direct training and co-developed 16 new use cases across 14 countries under the thematic areas of coastal adaptation, flood disaster preparedness, forestry and land restoration and water quality. Countries included: Madagascar, Mauritania, Rwanda, Djibouti, Gambia, Uganda, Senegal, Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Niger, Togo, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire, and the Democratic Republic of Congo.

title.narrative: Climate adaptation, mitigation, environment and biodiversity

description.narrative: Kenya’s expansive rangelands are critical to environmental and economic opportunities but are experiencing significant degradation due to climate change and unsustainable farming methods. The Northern Rangelands Trust (NRT) works with community groups to restore the rangelands through measures including sustainable grazing, replanting and invasive species control. ‍ DE Africa allows NRT to monitor vegetation and degradation patterns through free Earth observation datasets. NRT can compare vegetation health over time and geography, analysing trends in green space to identify areas of improvement under restoration measures, and areas where degradation remains a concern.

description.narrative: Natural hazards and human activities have contributed to increasing risk of coastal erosion, which impacts infrastructure, communities and livelihoods. ‍ DE Africa was used in a coastal erosion monitoring study in Comoros in late 2024. The Earth observation data available through the platform informed identification of 89 coastal erosion hotspots across the country. The insights from this study will assist decision-makers to develop specific interventions to prevent further erosion and restore areas with existing degradation.

description.narrative: The highest mountain in Kenya - and the second highest on the African continent - Mount Kenya is enclosed within the Mount Kenya National Park which covers an area of 715 km2 in the central highlands of the country. The National Park and Forest Reserve was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997 and is key in both local and international tourism to Kenya. ‍ DE Africa helped Eric Nganga, data technician at the Regional Center for Mapping of Resources for Development (RCMRD), to generate an assessment of the burnt area from 2019 forest fires to around 90 km2 (about 10% of the area). This was used in engagement with the Kenya Forest Service which is mandated with the task of monitoring forest cover. His work helped to inform policymakers in their efforts to conserve the forest and helps Kenya to report on the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals.
